questions.prompt: What is Project Quality Management?
options: The systematic process of planning, managing and controlling quality throughout a project life cycle
The inspection of a finished deliverable at the end of the project
A method of reducing project costs by cutting back on testing
The set of rules a client uses to approve project payments
questions.explanation: Project Quality Management covers planning, managing and controlling quality across the whole life cycle, not just a final check. Its purpose is to make sure deliverables meet requirements, standards and stakeholder expectations.

questions.prompt: A project finishes on time and within budget. What does the lecture say about its success?
options: It is a success, because time and cost are the only measures that count
It can still fail if its deliverables do not satisfy the required standards
It is guaranteed to have met every quality requirement
It can only fail if the client complains after handover
questions.explanation: Quality sits alongside time and cost. A deliverable that misses the required standards fails the project even when the schedule and budget were met.

questions.prompt: How do the lecture notes define quality?
options: The level of luxury or finish that a deliverable has
How cheaply a deliverable can be produced and delivered
The degree to which a deliverable fulfils stated requirements and is fit for its intended purpose
How quickly a deliverable is completed after approval
questions.explanation: Quality is about meeting stated requirements and being fit for purpose. It is not about luxury, low cost or speed.

questions.prompt: A machine runs for long periods without frequent breakdowns. Which dimension of quality does this show?
options: Conformance
Maintainability
Safety
Reliability
questions.explanation: Reliability is the ability to perform consistently. Conformance is compliance with specifications, and maintainability is how easily something can be repaired and serviced.

questions.prompt: Which principle says that all project participants share responsibility for quality?
options: Customer focus
Engagement of people
Process approach
Relationship management
questions.explanation: Under engagement of people, quality is not left to one inspector. Everyone who takes part in the project shares responsibility for it.

questions.prompt: What is quality assurance (QA)?
options: Activities designed to give confidence that quality requirements will be fulfilled
Inspecting and testing finished deliverables to find defects
The established requirements against which outputs are judged
The extent to which the final product meets client expectations
questions.explanation: QA focuses on the processes used to produce deliverables and aims to prevent defects. Inspecting finished outputs is quality control.

questions.prompt: What is quality control (QC)?
options: Audits that review how a contractor carries out its work
Writing the quality plan at the start of the project
Inspection, measurement and testing of deliverables to see whether they meet specified requirements
Training staff to follow the approved procedures
questions.explanation: QC examines the actual outputs. Audits and training belong to quality assurance, and writing the plan belongs to quality planning.

questions.prompt: What is the main output of quality planning?
options: A set of inspection reports and laboratory test results
A record of defects and the corrective actions taken
A signed certificate of client acceptance for the deliverable
A project quality management plan and supporting documentation
questions.explanation: Quality planning produces the plan and its supporting documents. Inspection reports, test results and defect records are typical outputs of quality control.

questions.prompt: Which tool ranks problems by frequency or impact so the biggest sources of defects are tackled first?
options: Pareto chart
Histogram
Flowchart
Check sheet
questions.explanation: A Pareto chart supports prioritisation and is linked to the 80/20 principle. The other tools show distribution, process steps or recorded observations.

questions.prompt: What is a cause-and-effect (fishbone) diagram used for?
options: Tracking measurements over time against upper and lower control limits
Showing how often measured values fall within each range
Recording observations of defects on a prepared form
Identifying possible root causes of a quality problem by grouping them into categories
questions.explanation: The fishbone groups possible causes under headings such as people, methods, materials, machines, measurement and environment.

questions.prompt: What does ISO 9001 specify?
options: Guidance on auditing management systems
Guidance on quality management in projects
Requirements for a quality management system
Fundamentals and vocabulary for quality management
questions.explanation: ISO 9001 gives requirements for a quality management system. ISO 19011 covers auditing, ISO 10006 covers projects, and ISO 9000 gives fundamentals and vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Which standard provides guidance on quality management in projects?
options: ISO 9000
ISO 9001
questions.explanation: ISO 10006 is the project-focused guidance. ISO 9000 is vocabulary, ISO 19011 is auditing, and ISO 9001 is the requirements standard.

questions.prompt: In the PDCA cycle, what does the letter C stand for?
options: Control
Confirm
Check
Complete
questions.explanation: PDCA stands for Plan, Do, Check, Act. In the Check step you measure results and compare them with expected performance.

questions.prompt: Testing concrete cube samples to verify compressive strength is an example of which activity?
options: Quality planning
Quality assurance
Continuous improvement
Quality control
questions.explanation: Testing actual samples against a specified requirement is quality control. Auditing the mixing procedure would be quality assurance.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a prevention cost?
options: Training project staff
Warranty claims after delivery
Scrap and rework before delivery
Inspecting finished work
questions.explanation: Training stops defects from being made, so it is a prevention cost. Inspection is an appraisal cost, rework is an internal failure cost, and warranty claims are an external failure cost.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly describes the main focus of QA and QC?
options: QA focuses on products and deliverables, while QC focuses on processes and systems
QA focuses on processes and systems, while QC focuses on products and deliverables
Both QA and QC focus only on finished deliverables
QA focuses on standards and procedures, while QC focuses on suppliers
questions.explanation: Assurance improves the processes used to produce quality, and control verifies whether the resulting outputs meet requirements. The two complement each other.

questions.prompt: A project manager organises casting, curing and testing as linked steps, each with defined inputs, procedures and outputs. Which principle does this reflect?
options: Leadership
Improvement
Relationship management
Process approach
questions.explanation: The process approach manages activities as interconnected processes with defined inputs, procedures and outputs.

questions.prompt: A project manager turns the client's needs into measurable requirements. Which principle does this reflect?
options: Customer focus
Leadership
Evidence-based decision-making
Improvement
questions.explanation: Customer focus means understanding client needs and translating them into measurable requirements.

questions.prompt: How should the 80/20 principle linked to Pareto charts be understood?
options: It is a fixed law that exactly 20 percent of causes produce 80 percent of defects
It means 80 percent of the project budget should go to testing
It is a guide that a few causes produce most problems, but the actual distribution varies
It means 20 percent of deliverables can skip inspection
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that the Pareto chart is associated with 80/20, although the actual distribution varies from project to project.

questions.prompt: What does a control chart help a project team do?
options: Rank defect types by how often they occur
Tell routine variation apart from possible special causes
List the items that must be verified before work proceeds
Map the sequence of activities and handovers in a process
questions.explanation: A control chart tracks measurements over time against a centre line and statistically calculated upper and lower control limits.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a check sheet and a checklist?
options: A check sheet lists items that must be verified, while a checklist records observations
A check sheet ranks problems, while a checklist shows variation over time
They are the same tool under two different names
A check sheet records observations systematically, while a checklist lists items that must be verified
questions.explanation: Recording cracks, surface defects and incomplete work during an inspection uses a check sheet. A checklist makes sure required items are verified.

questions.prompt: What does a histogram show?
options: The order of steps and decisions in a process
The frequency distribution of measured values, revealing variability, spread and patterns
The ranking of defects from most to least frequent
The groups of causes behind a quality problem
questions.explanation: A histogram helps the team understand variability and spread in process performance.

questions.prompt: Why would a team draw a flowchart of a process?
options: To rank defect types by their impact
To track measurements against control limits
To spot bottlenecks, unnecessary steps and opportunities for improvement
To estimate the cost of failures
questions.explanation: A flowchart shows the sequence of activities, decisions and handovers, which makes weak points in the process easier to see.

questions.prompt: What does ISO 9001 certification show about an organisation?
options: Its quality management system was assessed against the standard, within the scope of the certification
Every deliverable it produces is free of defects
Its projects will always finish within budget
It is exempt from national building codes and technical specifications
questions.explanation: Certification does not automatically guarantee that every deliverable is defect-free. Construction and engineering projects may still need to meet building codes and other requirements.

questions.prompt: Which costs together make up the cost of conformance?
options: Internal failure costs and external failure costs
Prevention costs and appraisal costs
Prevention costs and internal failure costs
Appraisal costs and external failure costs
questions.explanation: Prevention and appraisal are the costs of conformance. Internal and external failure costs are the costs of non-conformance.

questions.prompt: Which example is an external failure cost?
options: Warranty claims and compensation after delivery
Rework found before delivery
Repeated testing before handover
Audits of production procedures
questions.explanation: External failure costs arise when defects are found after delivery, such as warranty claims, repairs, compensation and reputational damage.

questions.prompt: A building complies with fire-safety requirements. Which dimension of quality does this show?
options: Performance
Durability
Safety
Maintainability
questions.explanation: Safety is the protection of people and property. Fire-safety compliance is the lecture's example for it.

questions.prompt: Which sequence matches the quality risk response described in the lecture?
options: Wait for defects to appear, assign blame, then replace the supplier
Assess consequences, ignore unlikely risks, then inspect only at the end
Assign responsible persons first, then identify risks after handover
Identify risks early, assess likelihood and consequences, assign responsible persons, and set preventive and corrective actions
questions.explanation: Quality risks are handled by early identification, assessment, clear ownership, and actions to prevent and correct problems.

questions.prompt: What happens in the Do step of the PDCA cycle?
options: Results are measured and compared with expected performance
The proposed solution is implemented, preferably on a controlled or limited scale
A problem is identified and its causes are analysed
Successful improvements are made the standard
questions.explanation: Plan sets the target, Do tries the fix, Check measures results, and Act standardises or revises the approach.

questions.prompt: What does the first-pass yield indicator measure?
options: The proportion of outputs that were inspected
The money spent correcting defective work
The time taken to resolve identified quality problems
The proportion of outputs that meet requirements without rework
questions.explanation: First-pass yield shows how much work is right first time. The money spent on fixes is rework cost, and the time to resolve problems is corrective-action closure time.

questions.prompt: A project has prevention costs of ₦200,000, appraisal costs of ₦100,000, internal failure costs of ₦400,000 and external failure costs of ₦300,000. What is its cost of non-conformance?
questions.explanation: Cost of non-conformance is internal plus external failure costs, which is ₦400,000 + ₦300,000 = ₦700,000. The ₦300,000 figure is the cost of conformance, and ₦1,000,000 is the total cost of quality.

questions.prompt: A project's cost of conformance is ₦800,000 and its cost of non-conformance is ₦1,200,000. What does the lecture suggest the project should do?
options: Investigate whether additional preventive measures could reduce defects and rework
Stop all prevention spending, since failures cost more
Treat quality as satisfactory, since conformance costs are lower
Ignore the figures, since some failure costs are always expected
questions.explanation: Failure costs larger than the money spent on conformance point to defects and rework that better prevention might reduce.

questions.prompt: On a building project, some concrete samples fail the specified compressive strength. Which response is most consistent with the lecture?
options: Retest the samples until a passing result appears, then continue work
Restrict affected work where necessary, verify results, find the root cause and have qualified professionals assess the affected elements
Cover the affected elements and continue so the completion date is kept
Continue working and record the failure in the final project report
questions.explanation: Work resumes only when authorised safety and quality requirements are met. Structural concerns must be assessed by qualified professionals.

questions.prompt: An audit shows that a contractor's concrete batching is inconsistent, before any defective concrete has been produced. What does this illustrate?
options: Quality control detecting a non-conformity in finished work
Quality planning setting acceptance criteria
Quality assurance acting to prevent defects
An external failure cost caused by a client complaint
questions.explanation: Reviewing a process before defective output exists is preventive, which is the role of quality assurance.

questions.prompt: A road surface performs well when new but cracks badly after one season of the traffic it was designed for. Which dimension of quality is mainly lacking?
options: Maintainability
Customer satisfaction
Conformance
Durability
questions.explanation: Durability is the ability to withstand use over time. The lecture's example is a road that withstands expected traffic.

questions.prompt: On a control chart, one measurement falls outside the upper control limit. How should the team interpret this?
options: It may point to a special cause that should be investigated, rather than routine variation
It confirms that the process is working normally
It proves that the deliverable is defective
It shows that the centre line was calculated wrongly
questions.explanation: Control charts help distinguish routine variation from potential special causes. A point outside the limits is a signal to investigate.

questions.prompt: A manager cuts the testing and training budget to save money. Using the cost-of-quality idea, what is the likely result?
options: All four cost categories fall together
Failure costs fall, because fewer defects are recorded
The cost of non-conformance becomes zero
Prevention and appraisal costs fall, but failure costs such as rework and warranty claims may rise
questions.explanation: Prevention reduces defects and rework. Cutting it can save conformance costs in the short term, but failures then cost more. The notes list conflicts between cost reduction and quality as a challenge.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the orientation of quality planning, QA and QC is correct?
options: Planning establishes requirements, QA is mainly preventive, and QC is mainly detective and corrective
Planning is mainly corrective, QA is mainly detective, and QC is mainly preventive
All three activities are mainly preventive in orientation
Planning is mainly detective, QA is mainly corrective, and QC is mainly preventive
questions.explanation: Planning sets the requirements, QA prevents problems through better processes, and QC finds and corrects problems in actual outputs.

questions.prompt: A contractor with ISO 9001 certification delivers some defective concrete. Why is this not a contradiction?
options: Certification applies only to the design stage of a project
Certification stops applying once a project begins
Certification shows its quality system was assessed, not that every deliverable is defect-free
Certification covers only contractors working outside their own country
questions.explanation: ISO 9001 certification is about the quality management system within its scope. It does not guarantee a defect-free deliverable.

questions.prompt: According to the lecture's conclusion, who is responsible for quality on a project?
options: Only the quality-control officer who inspects the work
It is a management responsibility built into governance, procurement, risk, scheduling, budgeting and stakeholder engagement
Only the client, who approves the final deliverable
Only the supplier, who produces the materials
questions.explanation: Quality is not only the job of an inspector. It is integrated into how the whole project is managed, and all participants share responsibility.

questions.prompt: A manufacturing project produces defective components. Which grouping of possible causes fits a fishbone diagram?
options: People, methods, materials, machines, measurement and environment
Price, place, promotion and product
Plan, do, check and act
Prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure
questions.explanation: A fishbone groups possible causes under categories such as people, methods, materials, machines, measurement and environment. The other lists belong to marketing, PDCA and cost of quality.

questions.prompt: A team pilots a new curing method on one floor, measures better strength results, and adopts the method on all floors. Which PDCA step is the adoption on all floors?
options: Plan
Do
Act
Check
questions.explanation: The pilot is Do, the measurement is Check, and making the successful change the standard is Act.

questions.prompt: A project reports a 98 percent inspection pass rate and calls its quality excellent. Why is this claim weak?
options: Inspection pass rate is not a recognised quality indicator
No single indicator can adequately represent overall project quality
A pass rate above 90 percent is never reliable
Only customer satisfaction counts as evidence of quality
questions.explanation: Indicators should be chosen to fit the project's scope, risks and objectives, and a single one cannot show overall quality.

questions.prompt: A supplier delivers substandard cement. Which earlier measures would best have reduced this risk?
options: Faster delivery schedules and larger orders
A larger quality-control team at the end of the project
Longer warranty clauses and delayed payments
Supplier qualification, approved specifications, incoming inspection and laboratory testing
questions.explanation: These four measures are the lecture's response to the risk of substandard materials. They act before the cement is used in the work.

questions.prompt: Workers hide defects because they fear being blamed. Which measure does the lecture recommend?
options: Encourage reporting of defects without inappropriate blame
Penalise every reported defect to deter errors
Move all inspection to the end of the project
Reduce the number of quality records kept
questions.explanation: Defects that are hidden cannot be corrected or learned from. The lecture lists blame-free reporting among the measures for overcoming quality challenges.
